title: Can an anonymous class extend a class and implement an interface simultaneously?
shortTitle: Can an anonymous class extend a class and implement an interface simultaneously?
keyPoints: An anonymous class names exactly one supertype in its declaration, so it can extend one class or implement one interface, never both.
The `new Type() { }` syntax has no slot for a combined `extends` and `implements` clause.
An anonymous object can still be a subclass and an interface implementer if the extended class already implements that interface transitively.
The workaround is to define a combined interface that extends multiple interfaces and implement that single combined interface anonymously.
When you genuinely need both class extension and new interface implementation, use a named class instead.
This single-supertype rule keeps the inline syntax simple and unambiguous.

s1_definition.oneliner: An anonymous class takes exactly one supertype, so it can never extend a class and implement an interface at the same time.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Single supertype rule** – the `new Type() { ... }` syntax names exactly one class or one interface, with no place for a combined `extends`/`implements` clause.
- **Class-based anonymous** – when `Type` is a class, the anonymous class extends that class and may use its constructor arguments.
- **Interface-based anonymous** – when `Type` is an interface, the anonymous class implements that one interface with an empty argument list.
- **Transitive interfaces** – an anonymous object can satisfy an interface only if the single superclass already implements it.
- **Workaround** – define a combined interface that `extends` multiple interfaces, then implement the combined interface anonymously.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a temporary helper at National Bank of India who is given a single job slip. The slip can say either "act as a Teller" or "follow the Auditor rulebook," but it physically has room for only one role. If Rajesh needs someone who is both a Teller and follows the Auditor rulebook, he must formally hire a named employee whose contract lists both roles. The nameless one-slip helper can wear only one hat.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│    Anonymous Class: Single Supertype Rule    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                             │
│   new SuperType(args) { body }              │
│        │                                    │
│        ├── SuperType is a class?            │
│        │     └── Extends that class         │
│        │         (inherits its interfaces)  │
│        │                                    │
│        └── SuperType is an interface?       │
│              └── Implements that interface  │
│                  (args must be empty)       │
│                                             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                             │
│   Need both class + interface?              │
│        │                                    │
│        ├── Transitive: base class already   │
│        │   implements the interface → OK    │
│        │                                    │
│        ├── Combine interfaces into one      │
│        │   combined interface → OK          │
│        │                                    │
│        └── Otherwise: use named class       │
│                                             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An anonymous class cannot extend a class and implement an interface at the same time, because the anonymous syntax names exactly one supertype. When you write `new SomeType() { body }`, `SomeType` is either a single class or a single interface, and there is no place for a second extends or implements clause. A named class, by contrast, can extend one class and implement many interfaces.

There is one subtle case that interviewers like to probe. An anonymous object can end up being both a subclass instance and an interface implementer, but only when the single class being extended already implements that interface. In a banking project a settlement task that implements Schedulable can be anonymously subclassed, and the resulting object is both a settlement task and a Schedulable, but the interface came transitively from the base class, not from a second supertype declaration.

When you genuinely need a throwaway object that satisfies two independent contracts, the clean solution is to define one combined interface that extends both, because interfaces are allowed to extend multiple interfaces. Then implement that single combined interface anonymously, supplying both method sets. That respects the one-supertype rule while still giving you both behaviours.

When you must extend a concrete class and implement a brand-new interface at the same time, there is no anonymous way to express it, so you write a named class. In practice this is also better for a bank's codebase because named classes are easier to test, easier to read, and easier to reuse.

Remember one sentence: an anonymous class takes exactly one supertype, so it can never extend a class and implement an interface at the same time; use a combined interface or a named class when you need both.
